primary_topics: Keynote address at the launch of 'Techniques and Ideals of the Filipino Lawyer' by Jose W. Diokno (updated by his son Jose Manuel I. Diokno), February 26, 2007 -- on Diokno's 85th birthday and the eve of his 20th death anniversary

Diokno's trial technique principle: three things necessary to win a case (good case, good lawyer, good judge) -- the lawyer can guarantee the first two, not the third; CJP's stress on the importance of the third

The 1960 Pasay CFI incident: CJP, substituting for Dean Salonga, faced Atty. Diokno on the other side; Diokno moved to postpone the hearing in fairness to the young, nervous lawyer -- 'urbanity and genial sportsmanship'

Diokno as a man of moral courage beyond honesty: initially supported Marcos (twice; same party; helped him); but when Marcos veered from the straight and narrow path, Ka Pepe denounced his excesses at personal risk
sub_topics: Book overview: the compilation discusses trial techniques for oral and documentary evidence; overcoming problems in evidence presentation; trial checklists and forms; 'a must read for all trial lawyers, both the young and old'

The three-things principle: according to Diokno, winning a case needs a good case, a good lawyer and a good judge; 'the first two, the lawyer could guarantee; the third, he could not'; CJP: 'having served in the Supreme Court for over 11 years, I can only stress on the significance of the third ingredient. Indeed, good lawyers need good judges who are ready to follow the law and do justice.'

The 1960 Pasay CFI encounter: immediately after passing the bar in 1960, CJP joined Salonga's law firm; one early morning, Salonga called to ask CJP to substitute for him in a trial at the CFI of Pasay; Atty. Diokno (plaintiff's counsel) generously moved to postpone in fairness to the young, inexperienced lawyer; 'this may have been a little incident in the checkered life of the legendary Atty. Jose W. Diokno, but it was a major one in mine'
Urbanity vs. moral courage: two distinct qualities of Diokno; urbanity (genial sportsmanship with a young nervous lawyer) is the lesser quality; the greater is moral courage

Honesty vs. integrity: during martial law, a 'handful kept themselves personally pure... Honesty is a virtue taught in grade school. But beyond honesty, the country needed men and women of integrity, who will not merely refuse to tell a falsehood, but who possess the moral courage to denounce a wrong and to promote the truth.'

Diokno's Marcos journey: twice supported Marcos's presidential candidacy; elected senator under the same party; initially helped him; but 'after it became clear that Marcos was veering from the straight and narrow path, Ka Pepe did not hesitate to part from him and to denounce his excesses. He could have kept quiet and tolerated the abuses. Instead, he worked fervently and actively, at the risk of his own safety, health, earthly possessions and career, to restore freedom in our land, to denounce the plunderers, to help the poor and to make truth and justice prevail.'

stances.claim: Jose W. Diokno's moral courage during martial law is qualitatively different from mere personal honesty. He initially supported Marcos -- twice and as a party colleague -- but denounced him when Marcos veered from the straight and narrow. This active denunciation at personal risk is the governing standard of integrity: not merely refusing to tell a falsehood, but actively opposing wrongdoing.
stances.rhetorical_move: honesty-vs-integrity-through-Diokno: the Marcos-supporter-turned-denouncer as the definitive behavioral example of the distinction
stances.confidence: asserted as the governing biographical evaluation

stances.claim: Good lawyers need good judges who are 'ready to follow the law and do justice' -- and this is the one ingredient in a case that lawyers cannot guarantee. CJP's stress on the judge's role (from 11 years of SC experience) elevates the judicial responsibility to equal standing with the lawyer's skill in determining case outcomes.
stances.rhetorical_move: the-third-ingredient argument: the judge's quality as the decisive and unguaranteed factor that lawyers must hope for but cannot control
stances.confidence: asserted as a judicial insider's observation

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered February 26, 2007 at the launch of 'Techniques and Ideals of the Filipino Lawyer' by Jose W. Diokno (updated by his son Jose Manuel I. Diokno) -- on Ka Pepe's 85th birthday and the eve of his 20th death anniversary -- this address by CJP uses Diokno as the governing illustration of the distinction between honesty and integrity. The book's governing principle: three things are necessary to win a case (good case, good lawyer, good judge); the lawyer can guarantee the first two but not the third; CJP from 11 SC years: 'good lawyers need good judges who are ready to follow the law and do justice.' He narrates the 1960 Pasay CFI encounter: as a newly minted lawyer substituting for Dean Salonga, CJP faced Atty. Diokno on the other side; Diokno moved to postpone the hearing in fairness to the young, nervous lawyer -- 'this may have been a little incident in the checkered life of the legendary Atty. Jose W. Diokno, but it was a major one in mine.' CJP identifies two qualities: urbanity (genial sportsmanship, the lesser) and moral courage (the deeper and greater). During martial law, some officials 'kept themselves personally pure' but did nothing -- 'honesty is a virtue taught in grade school.' Diokno demonstrated the higher standard: he initially supported Marcos twice (same party, elected senator, helped him) but when Marcos veered wrong, 'Ka Pepe did not hesitate to part from him and to denounce his excesses. He worked fervently and actively, at the risk of his own safety, health, earthly possessions and career, to restore freedom in our land, to denounce the plunderers, to help the poor and to make truth and justice prevail.' Conclusion: 'More than being honest, Jose Wright Diokno was a person of moral courage. He was moved by immutable values and principles, not by pettiness or convenience.'
